By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, it is hereby ordered:

Section 1.  Purpose.  The American Dream of homeownership is a vital pillar of our great country.  It is the policy of my Administration to reduce regulatory barriers to mortgage origination and costs impeding homeownership; embrace innovative risk and value assessment technologies that incorporate Super Intelligence to drive down mortgage and homeownership costs; and promote competition and innovation throughout the housing and mortgage market.

Sec. 2.  Proactive Cancellation of Excessive Mortgage Insurance.  (a)  The Director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency (Director) shall, if he determines that it is in the best interests of the Federal National Mortgage Association and the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation (Enterprises) or the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA), and the American public, direct the Enterprises to establish a pilot program, applicable only to mortgages made after the establishment of the pilot program, that periodically reviews single-family mortgage loans they own, guarantee, or securitize, using automated valuation models and other available data to assess current market value, and to identify borrowers who appear to satisfy equity and other requirements for cancellation of mortgage insurance.

(b)  The Director shall direct the Enterprises to establish procedures for the pilot program, including financial safety and soundness standards and payment-history requirements, under which mortgage insurance is canceled proactively when an Enterprise determines that:

(i)    the borrower satisfies applicable equity requirements based on the property’s current market value, as determined through an automated valuation model or other means approved by the Director;

(ii)   cancellation is consistent with financial safety and soundness and with the Enterprise’s contractual obligations; and

(iii)  the borrower satisfies all other applicable statutory, contractual, regulatory, and Enterprise requirements for cancellation.

(c)  The Director shall direct the Enterprises to require servicers, to the extent permitted by law and operationally feasible, to notify borrowers promptly when mortgage insurance may be canceled under the pilot program, and to reduce or eliminate unnecessary documentation requests, appraisal costs, and other administrative barriers to cancellation.

Sec. 3.  Standardizing the Permitting of Homes.  (a)  To increase the quality and lower the cost of building a home, there is hereby established the Task Force on Manufactured Housing Innovation (Task Force), which shall be co-chaired by the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development and the Director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, or their designees, and shall include the Secretary of Agriculture, the Secretary of Commerce, and the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, or their designees.  The co-chairs may invite the heads of other executive departments and agencies (agencies) to participate, as appropriate.

(b)  Within 180 days of the date of this order, the Task Force shall submit to the President, through the Assistant to the President for Economic Policy, recommendations to facilitate the use of modern manufacturing methods in the production of manufactured and other factory-built housing eligible for Federal housing programs, including actions to:

(i)    promote specifications, certifications, inspections, and approvals across Federal housing and housing-finance programs;

(ii)   establish reciprocal recognition among agencies of licenses, certifications, approvals, and inspections, where doing so would avoid unnecessary duplication;

(iii)  eliminate Federal requirements and duplicative reviews that unnecessarily impede automation, modularization, standardized production, or other advanced manufacturing techniques, or that increase the time or cost of bringing homes to market;

(iv)   use Federal financing, insurance, guarantee, purchasing, and other program authorities to encourage innovation and increased production of affordable manufactured and factory-built homes; and

(v)    promote competition among manufacturers and other market participants while maintaining appropriate standards for safety, quality, durability, and consumer protection.

(c)  The Task Force shall also evaluate whether, and under what existing statutory authorities, Federal grant funding may be conditioned on, or be used to incentivize, State and local adoption of standardized permitting and licensing for manufactured and other factory-built housing, consistent with the best practices issued under section 4(a) of Executive Order 14394 of March 13, 2026 (Removing Regulatory Barriers to Affordable Home Construction), and shall prepare legislative recommendations to codify the policies set forth in this subsection.

(d)  The heads of the agencies represented on the Task Force shall, within their respective authorities, take appropriate action to implement the Task Force’s recommendations.

Sec. 4.  Reducing Excessive Title Insurance, Especially in the Refinancing of Americans Homes.  (a)  The Director shall, if he determines that it is in the best interests of the Enterprises or the FHFA, and the American public, and consistent with financial safety and soundness, the Director’s authorities as regulator and conservator, and applicable law, direct the Enterprises to expand the title acceptance pilot into an ongoing program, available nationwide through both Enterprises, under which an Enterprise may accept an automated title review or other title-risk assessment approved by the FHFA in lieu of a lender’s title insurance policy on eligible refinance transactions.

(b)  In expanding the program, the Director shall consider:

(i)    extending eligibility to refinance transactions with loan-to-value ratios above the current 80 percent limit where title risk remains low;

(ii)   removing geographic limitations and certifying additional title-assessment providers to promote competition;

(iii)  waiving appraisals, income re-verification, and other documentation requirements for limited cash-out refinances that reduce the borrower’s monthly payment, where the Enterprise’s existing data support doing so; and

(iv)   reducing or eliminating loan-level price adjustments and other Enterprise fees on such refinances.

(c)  The Director shall require that cost savings resulting from the program be passed through to borrowers and that lenders inform borrowers of those savings.

Sec. 5.  Department of Agriculture and Department of Veterans Affairs Direct Loan Rates.  The Secretary of Agriculture and the Secretary of Veterans Affairs shall, consistent with applicable law, including 42 U.S.C. 1490a(a)(1)(B) and 38 U.S.C. 3762(c)(1), and available appropriations, reduce the interest rates charged on single‑family home loans made directly by their respective departments.

Sec. 6.  General Provisions.  (a)  Nothing in this order shall be construed to impair or otherwise affect:

(i)   the authority granted by law to an executive department or agency, or the head thereof; or

(ii)  the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget relating to budgetary, administrative, or legislative proposals.

(b)  This order shall be implemented consistent with applicable law and subject to the availability of appropriations.

(c)  This order is not intended to, and does not, create any right or benefit, substantive or procedural, enforceable at law or in equity by any party against the United States, its departments, agencies, or entities, its officers, employees, or agents, or any other person.

(d)  The costs for publication of this order shall be borne by the Federal Housing Finance Agency.

DONALD J. TRUMP

THE WHITE HOUSE,

         October 22, 2026.

By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, it is hereby ordered:

Section 1.  Purpose.  America stands at the forefront of a new technological revolution in intelligence.  The modern field of artificial intelligence was born in the United States, where American scientists first gave the field its name and laid the foundations for its development.  Seventy years later, powered by our Nation’s unmatched culture of innovation, world-leading companies and research institutions, and entrepreneurial spirit, America is once again pushing the technological frontier forward.

The extraordinary technologies being pioneered by American innovators far exceed what was envisioned when the term “Artificial Intelligence” first came into use.  The capabilities of today’s frontier systems do much more than imitate or automate discrete aspects of human intelligence.  They increasingly amplify human ingenuity and unlock new forms of creativity, empowering Americans to achieve what was previously impossible across science, medicine, and nearly every other domain of human endeavor.  As these capabilities continue to improve, they increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era of Super Intelligence.

The terminology used by the Federal Government should reflect the transformative capabilities of these technologies and the limitless opportunities they create for the American people.  Accordingly, the term “Super Intelligence” more appropriately captures the promise, potential, and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies.  It is therefore the policy of my Administration that, to the maximum extent permitted by law, the executive branch shall use the terms “Super Intelligence” and “SI” in place of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI” and will not acknowledge the usage of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI” in any applicable setting.

Sec. 2.  Implementation.  (a)  To the maximum extent permitted by law, executive departments and agencies (agencies) shall use “Super Intelligence” and “SI” in place of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI” in official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents, and other non-statutory documents within the executive branch.

(b)  Nothing in this section requires the alteration of previously issued regulations, Presidential actions, contracts, grants, or other historical documents.

Sec. 3.  Definition.  (a)  For purposes of this order, and except where otherwise provided by law, the terms “Super Intelligence” and “SI” mean the technologies and systems encompassed by the term “artificial intelligence” as defined in section 9401(3) of title 15, United States Code.  This definition shall govern the implementation of this order unless and until superseded by subsequent Presidential action consistent with applicable law or by an Act of Congress.

(b)  Within 60 days of the date of this order, the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology (APST), in consultation with the heads of other agencies as the APST deems appropriate, shall submit to the President proposed legislative language to establish a Federal definition of “Super Intelligence” and “SI” that reflects the capabilities described in section 1 of this order.  The proposal shall include:

(i)    an assessment of whether, and to what extent, the definition of “Super Intelligence” and “SI” should modify, expand upon, or otherwise supersede the existing statutory definition of “artificial intelligence”;

(ii)   any proposed conforming amendments, as appropriate, to existing statutory references to “artificial intelligence” and “AI”; and

(iii)  recommendations for any additional Presidential or executive action necessary to implement the proposed definition throughout the executive branch.

Sec. 4.  General Provisions.  (a)  Nothing in this order shall be construed to impair or otherwise affect:

(i)   the authority granted by law to an executive department or agency, or the head thereof; or

(ii)  the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget relating to budgetary, administrative, or legislative proposals.

(b)  This order shall be implemented consistent with applicable law and subject to the availability of appropriations.

(c)  This order is not intended to, and does not, create any right or benefit, substantive or procedural, enforceable at law or in equity by any party against the United States, its departments, agencies, or entities, its officers, employees, or agents, or any other person.

(d)  The costs for publication of this order shall be borne by the Office of Science and Technology Policy.

                              

DONALD J. TRUMP

THE WHITE HOUSE,     September 29, 2026.

item.dc:creator: The White House

BY THE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA

A PROCLAMATION

1.  Within the past 90 days, the Secretary of Commerce (Secretary) transmitted to me a report on his investigation into the effects of imports of robotics and industrial machinery, as well as their parts and components (together, components), on the national security of the United States under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended, 19 U.S.C. 1862 (section 232).  Based on the facts considered in that investigation, and taking into account the close relation of the economic welfare of the Nation to our national security and other relevant factors, see section 232(d) (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)), the Secretary found and advised me of his opinion that robotics, industrial machinery, and their components are being imported into the United States in such quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States.

2.  Nearly all modern defense systems and critical infrastructure sectors require the use of robotics or industrial machinery to function or be manufactured effectively and efficiently.  Robotics and industrial machinery are critical to virtually all modern manufacturing processes, including for defense, commercial, and dual-use purposes.  Robotics and industrial machinery enable defense readiness and design, production, and sustainment activities across a wide range of defense applications.  Furthermore, robotics and industrial machinery generate substantial economic value and support important economic activities, including approximately $7.1 trillion in shipments of manufactured goods in 2024 and the production of approximately $86 billion worth of equipment in 2024.  

3.  The Secretary found that robotics and industrial machinery support the production of essential, state-of-the-art defense systems, such as aircraft, tanks, ships, weapons, and munitions, as well as certain military and law enforcement activities.  For example, advanced robots — such as autonomous robots, humanoid and quadruped robots, and autonomous ground vehicles — provide combat support to the United States military, including by conducting intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions and by handling dangerous tasks, such as casualty extraction and mine detection and clearing.  Robotics and industrial machinery also enable the defense industry to automate the building of essential defense products, such as missiles, aircraft, and ships, allowing production activities to last longer and for repetitive tasks to be performed with minimal error.  Indeed, the defense industrial base’s ability to surge production, including during wartime or armed conflict, relies on industrial robotics and machinery.

4.  The Secretary found that robotics and industrial machines are also crucial to the United States’ critical infrastructure sectors and other key aspects of the United States economy.  Industrial robots and machines are used to create products and parts that are used across all 16 critical infrastructure sectors of the United States.  For example, industrial robots are heavily used in the automotive, electrical, and electronics industries and are also meaningfully used in the metal and machinery, plastic and chemical products, and food and beverage industries.  Similarly, industrial machinery carries out critical functions across various industries and in the manufacturing process for a range of goods, including construction equipment, electronics, medical devices, metal fabrication, motor vehicles, and aircraft.  And because industrial robots and machinery serve end-use industries and contribute to equipment manufacturing and product creation efforts, they carry expansive downstream implications for the United States economy.  Thus, robotics and industrial machines are a driving force behind critical infrastructure sectors and are crucial to the national and economic security interests of the United States.

5.  The Secretary found that the United States relies on foreign imports for most types of robotics and industrial machinery and for their components.  The value of robotics, industrial machinery, and their components imported into the United States has increased over the last decade and is projected to continue to increase.  This import reliance poses risks to the United States industrial base and threatens the long-term competitiveness of the United States in a sector that is increasingly vital to national security.

6.  The Secretary also found that robotics, industrial machinery, and their components from certain foreign entities pose unique security and safety risks.  Robotics and industrial machinery are integrated into many manufacturing and defense systems and routinely process and store sensitive data.  These technologies, when sourced from foreign entities, can pose significant cybersecurity vulnerabilities that can result in severe consequences to the United States. 

7.  The Secretary found that the domestic industry does not produce enough robotics, industrial machinery, and their components to meet national security needs, and that the need for domestically produced robotics, industrial machinery, and their components will only increase.  Despite a recent surge in investments in manufacturing facilities in the United States, the United States still produces less robotics and industrial equipment than it consumes, lacks the capacity to satisfy the need for robotics and industrial machinery with domestic sources, and underutilizes its manufacturing capacity for robotics, industrial equipment, and their components.  According to the Secretary, without intervention, challenges for United States manufacturers investing in robotics and industrial machinery will likely continue.  In the Secretary’s opinion, it is vital to take action to strengthen, expand, and modernize the domestic manufacturing and industrial base for robotics, industrial machinery, and their components.

8.  In light of these findings and other findings in the Secretary’s report, the Secretary recommended various actions to adjust the imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and their components so that such imports will not threaten to impair the national security.

9.  After considering the Secretary’s report, the factors in section 232(d) (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)), and other relevant factors and information, I concur with the Secretary’s finding that robotics, industrial machinery, and their components are being imported into the United States in such quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States.  In my judgment, and in light of the Secretary’s report, the factors in section 232(d) (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)), and other relevant factors and information, I determine that it is necessary and appropriate to enter into negotiations with trading partners to adjust imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and their components so that such imports will not threaten to impair the national security of the United States.

10.  I therefore direct the Secretary and the United States Trade Representative (Trade Representative) to jointly pursue negotiations of agreements or continue any current negotiations of agreements to address the threatened impairment of the national security with respect to imported robotics, industrial machinery, and their components, with any foreign trading partner the Secretary and the Trade Representative deem appropriate, and to update me on the progress of such negotiations within 180 days of the date of this proclamation.  Under current circumstances and in light of future requirements of the United States, this course of action is necessary and appropriate to address the threatened impairment of the national security. 

11.  Section 232 authorizes the President to take action to adjust the imports of an article and its derivatives that are being imported into the United States in such quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security.  Section 232 includes the authority to adopt and carry out a plan of action, with adjustments over time, to address the national security threat.  That initial plan of action may include negotiations of agreements along with other actions to adjust imports to address the national security threat, including tariffs, duties, quotas, and fees.  If action under section 232 includes the negotiation of an agreement, such as one contemplated in section 232(c)(3)(A)(i) (19 U.S.C. 1862(c)(3)(A)(i)), the President may also take other actions he deems necessary to adjust imports to eliminate the threat that the imported article poses to the national security, including if such an agreement is not entered into within 180 days of the date of this proclamation, is not being carried out, or is ineffective.  See 19 U.S.C. 1862(c)(3)(A).

12.  Section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19 U.S.C. 2483) (section 604), authorizes the President to embody in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States the substance of statutes affecting import treatment, and actions thereunder, including the removal, modification, continuance, or imposition of any rate of duty or other import restriction.

NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of America, by the authority vested in me by the Constitution and the laws of the United States, including section 232; section 604; and section 301 of title 3, United States Code, do hereby proclaim as follows:

(1)  The Secretary and the Trade Representative shall jointly pursue or continue pursuing negotiations of agreements to address the threatened impairment of the national security with respect to imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and their components.  Depending on the status or outcome of such negotiations, I may consider alternative remedies in the future, including imposing or modifying tariffs, duties, quotas, and fees; and establishing a program to incentivize new investment in United States production of robotics and industrial machinery, as well as their parts and components.

     (2)  The Secretary and the Trade Representative, in consultation with any other senior executive branch official they deem appropriate, shall, from time to time, update me on the status or outcome of the negotiations described in this proclamation.  The Secretary and the Trade Representative shall provide one of these updates within 180 days of the date of this proclamation.

(3)  The Secretary shall continue to monitor imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and their components and shall, from time to time, in consultation with any senior executive branch officials the Secretary deems appropriate, review the status of such imports with respect to the national security.  The Secretary shall inform me of any circumstances that, in the Secretary’s opinion, might indicate the need for further action by the President under section 232.

(4)  Any provision of previous proclamations and Executive Orders that is inconsistent with this proclamation is superseded to the extent of such inconsistency.  If any provision of this proclamation or the application of any provision of this proclamation to any individual or circumstance is held to be invalid, the remainder of this proclamation and the application of its provisions to any other individual or circumstance shall not be affected.

     IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this

twenty-eighth day of October, in the year of our Lord two thousand twenty-six, and of the Independence of the United States of America the two hundred and fifty-first.

                             DONALD J. TRUMP

(4)  Any provision of previous proclamations and Executive Orders that is inconsistent with this proclamation is superseded to the extent of such inconsistency.  If any provision of this proclamation or the application of any provision of this proclamation to any individual or circumstance is held to be invalid, the remainder of this proclamation and the application of its provisions to any other individual or circumstance shall not be affected.

     IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this

twenty-eighth day of October, in the year of our Lord two thousand twenty-six, and of the Independence of the United States of America the two hundred and fifty-first.

                             DONALD J. TRUMP
